events.title: First Ebola Cases Detected in Yambuku, Zaire
events.detail: On 26 August 1976, a schoolteacher named Mabalo Lokela fell ill at Yambuku Mission Hospital in northern Zaire (now DRC) after returning from a trip along the Ebola River. Reused hypodermic needles at the mission hospital rapidly amplified transmission. By late October, 318 people had been infected and 280 had died — a case fatality rate of 88%. The virus was isolated and named Ebola after the nearby river.

sources.name: CDC — History of Ebola Virus Disease

events.title: Simultaneous Sudan Outbreak — Second Ebola Strain Identified
events.detail: Almost simultaneously with Yambuku, a separate outbreak erupted in Nzara, Sudan (now South Sudan) in June 1976, affecting cotton factory workers. This outbreak caused 284 cases and 151 deaths (CFR 53%). Laboratory analysis revealed a genetically distinct strain, later named Sudan ebolavirus (SUDV), confirming Ebola comprised multiple species. The two simultaneous outbreaks caused widespread scientific alarm.

events.title: International WHO Investigation Team Arrives in Yambuku
events.detail: An international team of scientists from WHO, CDC, and the Belgian Institute of Tropical Medicine arrived in October 1976 to investigate the Yambuku outbreak. They identified reused syringes at the mission hospital as the primary amplifying factor and implemented a strict quarantine that ended the outbreak. Researchers Karl Johnson and Peter Piot were among those who isolated and characterized the new pathogen, naming it Ebola virus.

sources.name: Lancet — Original Ebola Virus Isolation Report (1977)
CDC — History of Ebola Virus Disease

events.title: Reston Ebolavirus Discovered in US Primate Facility
events.detail: Cynomolgus macaques imported from the Philippines and housed at a primate facility in Reston, Virginia began dying in large numbers in October 1989. The CDC identified a new filovirus — Reston ebolavirus (RESTV). Although it spread among monkeys and several humans tested seropositive, no humans developed disease. RESTV remains the only Ebola species non-pathogenic to humans, but the event triggered sweeping changes to biosafety regulations for imported primates in the USA.

sources.name: CDC MMWR — Ebola-Like Virus Among Imported Macaques (1990)

events.title: Taï Forest Strain Found in Côte d'Ivoire
events.detail: In November 1994, a Swiss ethologist conducting chimpanzee research in the Taï National Forest, Côte d'Ivoire, developed Ebola-like symptoms after performing a necropsy on a dead chimpanzee. She was evacuated to Switzerland and survived. Virus isolated from her blood represented a fourth distinct Ebola species — Taï Forest ebolavirus (TAFV) — the rarest strain, with only this single confirmed human case.

events.title: Kikwit Outbreak — 315 Cases, 250 Deaths in DRC
events.detail: From January to July 1995, a major Ebola (Zaire strain) outbreak struck Kikwit, a city of 500,000 in the DRC. An initial cluster spread explosively through Kikwit General Hospital when infection-control precautions failed. Final toll: 315 cases, 250 deaths (CFR 79%). The outbreak attracted intense international media attention and prompted WHO to establish a global outbreak alert and response network. An index case linked to charcoal and cotton work in nearby forests suggested animal-to-human spillover.

sources.name: NEJM — Ebola Hemorrhagic Fever, Kikwit, DRC, 1995

events.title: Two Separate Ebola Outbreaks in Gabon
events.detail: Gabon experienced two separate Zaire ebolavirus outbreaks in 1996: one in Mayibout (31 cases, 21 deaths) linked to butchering a chimpanzee, and a second in Booué (60 cases, 45 deaths). A South African nurse who treated a patient from the Booué cluster died in Johannesburg — the first imported Ebola death outside Central Africa. Both outbreaks underscored the role of bushmeat handling as a zoonotic bridge.

events.title: Uganda's Largest Outbreak — Sudan Strain, 425 Cases
events.detail: From August 2000 to January 2001, Uganda's Gulu district suffered the largest Sudan ebolavirus outbreak on record, with 425 cases and 224 deaths (CFR 53%). The outbreak spread along a truck route from Gulu through Masindi to Mbarara. WHO and MSF deployed response teams and established isolation wards. The Ugandan government's rapid mobilization and community engagement were credited with containing the outbreak within six months.

events.title: Republic of Congo Outbreaks Kill Over 100
events.detail: Between 2001 and 2003, a series of overlapping Zaire ebolavirus outbreaks struck the Republic of Congo (Brazzaville), particularly in Mbomo district near the Odzala National Park. Combined cases across the 2001–2002 and 2002–2003 clusters exceeded 290, with approximately 200 deaths. Repeated outbreak detection in the same area — linked to gorilla and other wildlife die-offs — drew scientific attention to the role of great apes as sentinels for Ebola spillover.

sources.name: Science — Great Ape Ebola Mortality (Leroy et al.)

events.title: New Bundibugyo Strain Identified in Uganda
events.detail: In November 2007, an outbreak in Bundibugyo District, western Uganda was initially suspected to be Marburg or yellow fever. CDC laboratory analysis revealed an entirely new Ebola species — Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV) — representing only the fifth known Ebola strain. The outbreak caused 149 cases and 37 deaths (CFR 25%), notably lower than the Zaire strain. Bundibugyo's emergence near the DRC border set the stage for the 2026 cross-border outbreak.

events.title: DRC Kasai Occidental Outbreak — 264 Cases
events.detail: Simultaneously with the Bundibugyo Uganda outbreak, a separate Zaire ebolavirus outbreak erupted in Kasai Occidental Province, DRC in September 2007, causing 264 cases and 187 deaths (CFR 71%). The near-simultaneous emergence of two distinct Ebola strains in neighboring countries in the same month was unprecedented and prompted WHO to convene an expert panel on filovirus ecology.

sources.name: WHO DON — DRC Kasai Ebola Outbreak 2007

events.title: Uganda Sudan Strain Outbreak — Kibaale District
events.detail: In July 2012, a Sudan ebolavirus outbreak erupted in Kibaale District, Uganda, killing 17 of 24 confirmed cases (CFR 71%). A second, concurrent cluster in Luwero District added further complexity. Uganda's rapid response — including ring vaccination trials with an investigational VSV-based vaccine — provided early real-world data that informed later mass vaccination strategies. WHO commended Uganda's surveillance and response infrastructure.

events.title: DRC Isiro Outbreak — Bundibugyo Strain in Orientale Province
events.detail: In June 2012, a Bundibugyo ebolavirus outbreak struck Isiro, Orientale Province, DRC — the second confirmed emergence of this strain. The outbreak produced 77 cases and 36 deaths (CFR 47%). Cross-border surveillance was heightened given proximity to Uganda. This was the second and final confirmed Bundibugyo strain outbreak before the 2026 reemergence, making it a critical reference point for understanding BDBV epidemiology.

events.title: Index Case: 18-Month-Old Child Dies in Guéckédou, Guinea
events.detail: In December 2013, an 18-month-old boy named Emile Ouamouno in Meliandou village, Guéckédou Prefecture, Guinea, became ill and died on 6 December — later established as the index case for the West Africa epidemic. His mother, sister, and grandmother died shortly after, with the disease spreading silently for months along funeral networks and bush-taxi routes before being identified. The delayed recognition allowed the virus to reach Conakry and cross into Sierra Leone and Liberia before the outbreak was officially declared.

sources.name: NEJM — Emergence of Zaire Ebola Virus in Guinea (2014)
WHO — West Africa Ebola Epidemic Timeline

events.title: WHO Declares Ebola Outbreak in Guinea — March 2014
events.detail: On 22 March 2014, WHO officially declared the Ebola outbreak in Guinea after laboratory confirmation from Institut Pasteur Paris. By this date, the virus had already spread beyond the Guéckédou forest zone to the capital Conakry and had crossed the border into Liberia. MSF immediately classified the situation as 'unprecedented' for West Africa. The delayed official response — hampered by weak surveillance infrastructure and unfamiliarity with Ebola in the region — allowed community transmission to escalate rapidly.

sources.name: WHO DON — Ebola Virus Disease, Guinea

events.title: WHO Declares Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC)
events.detail: On 8 August 2014, WHO Director-General Margaret Chan declared the West Africa Ebola epidemic a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) — only the third PHEIC in WHO history. By this date, 1,711 cases and 932 deaths had been reported across Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone. The declaration triggered UN Security Council Resolution 2177 (September 2014), which described Ebola as a threat to international peace and security — unprecedented for a disease outbreak.

events.title: Liberia's Health System Collapses — August–September 2014
events.detail: By September 2014, Liberia had become the epicenter of the worst Ebola epidemic in history. Ebola Treatment Units (ETUs) in Monrovia were turning away patients. Bodies lay uncollected in the streets of West Point slum. MSF reported that 8 of 10 patients arriving at ETUs were dead before they could be admitted. Liberia's entire pre-crisis healthcare system — with only 51 physicians for 4.3 million people — collapsed. US President Obama deployed 3,000 troops to West Africa under Operation United Assistance to build ETUs and train healthcare workers.

sources.name: MSF — Appeal on West Africa Ebola

events.title: First Imported Ebola Case in the United States — Dallas, Texas
events.detail: On 30 September 2014, Thomas Eric Duncan became the first person diagnosed with Ebola in the United States, having traveled from Liberia to Dallas, Texas. Duncan died on 8 October. Two nurses who cared for him — Nina Pham and Amber Vinson — tested positive, becoming the first Ebola transmissions on US soil. The cases sparked intense media coverage, congressional hearings, and policy changes including enhanced airport screening. Both nurses recovered fully.

events.title: Accelerated Vaccine Trials Begin — rVSV-ZEBOV Enters Phase I
events.detail: In October 2014, WHO convened an emergency ethics panel that authorized use of experimental Ebola vaccines on compassionate grounds before Phase III trial completion. The rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine (Merck), originally developed by the Public Health Agency of Canada and licensed to NewLink Genetics, entered Phase I trials at the NIH. Parallel trials began for the ChAd3-EBO-Z (Oxford/GSK) and VSV-ZEBOV platforms. The aggressive push compressed a decade of normal development into months.

sources.name: The Lancet — rVSV-ZEBOV Trial (Agnandji et al., 2015)

events.title: Guinea Ring Vaccination Trial — rVSV-ZEBOV Shows 100% Efficacy
events.detail: The landmark Ebola Ça Suffit! ring vaccination trial in Guinea (April–July 2015) randomized 7,651 contacts of confirmed cases to immediate or delayed vaccination with rVSV-ZEBOV. Among those vaccinated immediately, zero cases occurred from day 10 onward. The Lancet reported 100% efficacy in the immediate arm, with a p-value < 0.0001 — described as 'one of the most decisive vaccine trials in history.' Results fundamentally changed outbreak response strategy and paved the way for WHO prequalification.

sources.name: The Lancet — Ebola Ça Suffit! Ring Vaccination Trial (Henao-Restrepo, 2015)

events.title: WHO Declares End of West Africa Ebola Epidemic — 28,616 Cases
events.detail: On 14 January 2016, WHO declared the end of the West Africa Ebola epidemic. Final toll: 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths across Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone — by far the largest Ebola outbreak in history. Additional imported cases occurred in Nigeria, Senegal, Spain, Italy, USA, UK, and Mali. The outbreak killed approximately 500 healthcare workers. A post-epidemic review by the Harvard Global Health Institute and London School of Hygiene found WHO's initial response was 'too slow' and led to major organizational reforms.

sources.name: WHO — End of Ebola West Africa Statement

events.title: DRC Équateur Outbreak Contained — rVSV Deployed First Time
events.detail: On 8 May 2018, DRC declared its 9th Ebola outbreak in Bikoro, Équateur Province, followed by spread to the river town of Mbandaka. This was the first outbreak in which rVSV-ZEBOV was deployed outside a clinical trial under expanded access. Gavi allocated $1 million from the Ebola stockpile for 4,240 doses. WHO and DRC MoH conducted ring vaccination of contacts. The outbreak was declared over on 24 July 2018 with 54 cases and 33 deaths.

events.title: 10th DRC Outbreak Declared in North Kivu — Becomes Largest in DRC History
events.detail: On 1 August 2018, DRC declared its 10th Ebola outbreak in North Kivu Province — a conflict zone where over 100 armed groups operated. The Kivu outbreak became the second-largest Ebola outbreak in history, lasting nearly two years (August 2018 – June 2020) and producing 3,481 cases and 2,299 deaths. The active conflict, community distrust, and anti-vaccination sentiment severely hampered response. At least 7 healthcare workers were killed by armed groups, and Ebola Treatment Units were attacked on multiple occasions.

sources.name: MSF — Violence Against Ebola Response DRC

events.title: WHO Declares Second PHEIC for DRC Kivu Outbreak
events.detail: On 17 July 2019, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus declared the DRC Kivu outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern — the sixth PHEIC in WHO history. The declaration came after a confirmed case was identified in Goma, a city of 1 million on the Rwanda border with a major international airport. The delayed PHEIC declaration (the Emergency Committee had rejected PHEIC status three times in 2018–2019) drew criticism from some global health experts.

events.title: DRC Kivu Outbreak Declared Over — 3,481 Cases, 2,299 Deaths
events.detail: On 25 June 2020, WHO declared the end of the DRC Kivu Ebola outbreak — the world's second-largest and most prolonged Ebola outbreak in history. During 25 months, the response mobilized over 30,000 community health workers, administered approximately 303,000 rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine doses, and fielded the first deployments of two additional vaccines (Ad26.ZEBOV/MVA-BN-Filo). Clinical trials also established that antibody cocktails (mAb114 and REGN-EB3) reduced Kivu mortality to under 30%.

sources.name: WHO — End of DRC Kivu Ebola Outbreak
NEJM — Therapeutics in Kivu Outbreak (Mulangu et al.)

events.title: DRC 11th Outbreak Erupts During COVID-19 Pandemic — Équateur Province
events.detail: On 1 June 2020 — just one week before the Kivu outbreak was declared over — DRC announced its 11th Ebola outbreak in Mbandaka, Équateur Province. The simultaneous collision with the COVID-19 pandemic response created severe strain on DRC's health system, with personnel, PPE, and community trust all being divided between two crises. The outbreak produced 130 cases and 55 deaths (CFR 42%) before being declared over on 18 November 2020. WHO deployed rapid ring vaccination with rVSV-ZEBOV within 72 hours of outbreak declaration.

sources.name: WHO DON — DRC Ebola Équateur June 2020
Reuters — DRC New Ebola Outbreak During COVID-19

events.title: Guinea 2021 Outbreak — First West Africa Reemergence in 5 Years
events.detail: On 14 February 2021, Guinea declared an Ebola outbreak in Nzérékoré, southern Guinea — the first in West Africa since the 2016 epidemic end. Genomic sequencing revealed the virus was not a new spillover but derived from a survivor of the 2014–2016 epidemic who harbored the virus for five years — the longest documented persistence in a survivor. The outbreak produced 23 cases and 12 deaths before containment. This finding raised major questions about long-term viral persistence and reopened debates on survivor monitoring.

sources.name: Nature — Guinea Ebola Resurgence from Survivor (Diallo et al., 2021)

events.title: Uganda Sudan Strain Outbreak — No Available Vaccine, 55 Deaths
events.detail: On 20 September 2022, Uganda declared an outbreak of Sudan ebolavirus (SUDV) in Mubende District. Unlike Zaire ebolavirus, no licensed vaccine existed for SUDV. WHO and partners rapidly initiated trials of four candidate SUDV vaccines, but none were ready for deployment before the outbreak was contained. Final toll: 164 cases and 55 deaths. The outbreak exposed a critical gap in the global outbreak preparedness portfolio: vaccines had focused almost exclusively on the Zaire strain despite six known Ebola species.

sources.name: Reuters — Uganda Ebola Sudan Strain Vaccine Gap 2022

events.title: DRC 16th Outbreak Declared — Équateur Province, EBOV
events.detail: In April 2023, DRC declared its 16th Ebola outbreak, again in Équateur Province — the seventh outbreak in that province since 2018. Fourteen cases and six deaths were reported. Ring vaccination with rVSV-ZEBOV was initiated within 48 hours of case confirmation. The outbreak was declared over in June 2023. The repeated Équateur emergences suggested persistent forest reservoir activity and challenged assumptions that vaccination campaigns alone could break the zoonotic transmission cycle.

events.title: Bundibugyo Strain Detected in Ituri Province, DRC — December 2025
events.detail: In December 2025, DRC health authorities and WHO confirmed Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV) in samples from three patients in Mahagi Territory, Ituri Province — the first confirmed BDBV detection in DRC and only the third known BDBV outbreak globally. Epidemiological investigation linked the index cluster to bushmeat hunting near the DRC-Uganda border forest zone. Genomic sequencing confirmed phylogenetic proximity to the 2012 Isiro DRC isolate, suggesting spillover from a reservoir persisting in the Ituri forest ecosystem.

sources.name: WHO Disease Outbreak News — BDBV DRC December 2025

events.title: DRC Ministry of Health Declares 17th Ebola Outbreak — January 2026
events.detail: On 7 January 2026, DRC Minister of Health formally declared an Ebola outbreak in Ituri Province, activating the National Ebola Response Plan. By declaration date, 12 confirmed and 9 probable cases had been identified across three health zones in Mahagi, Djugu, and Irumu Territories. WHO deployed a GOARN team and CDC an Emergency Operations surge team within 24 hours. Ring vaccination with rVSV-ZEBOV was authorized, though vaccine stocks for Bundibugyo strain were flagged as experimental.

sources.name: WHO Situation Report — DRC Ebola January 2026
DRC Ministry of Health — Communiqué Officiel

events.title: Cross-Border Cases Confirmed in Uganda — Bundibugyo District
events.detail: On 18 February 2026, Uganda's Ministry of Health confirmed three cases of Bundibugyo ebolavirus in Bundibugyo District — the same geographic region where BDBV was first discovered in 2007. All three cases had recent travel histories linking them to Ituri Province market networks. Uganda activated its Emergency Operations Center, instituted border health screening at all DRC-Uganda crossings, and began contact tracing of 87 exposed individuals. Cross-border coordination between DRC and Uganda MoH was established via WHO IHR Emergency Focal Point channels.

sources.name: Uganda Ministry of Health — Ebola Alert
BBC — Ebola Spreads to Uganda February 2026

events.title: Ring Vaccination Campaign Launched — rVSV-ZEBOV + Investigational BDBV Vaccine
events.detail: On 5 March 2026, WHO and DRC MoH launched a ring vaccination campaign targeting all identified contacts and contacts of contacts in Ituri Province. A total of 12,800 doses of rVSV-ZEBOV (licensed for Zaire strain, used off-label given partial cross-protection data) and 3,000 doses of an investigational BDBV-targeted MVA-BN-Filo formulation were shipped under emergency use protocol. Coverage of ring contacts reached 74% by end of March. WHO noted that rVSV-ZEBOV had demonstrated partial protection against BDBV in non-human primate models.

sources.name: GAVI — Emergency Ebola Vaccine Supply DRC 2026

events.title: WHO Emergency Committee Convenes — PHEIC Assessment for 2026 Outbreak
events.detail: On 14 April 2026, WHO Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus convened the International Health Regulations Emergency Committee to assess whether the 2026 DRC-Uganda Bundibugyo outbreak constitutes a PHEIC. The committee noted: (1) cross-border spread confirmed in Uganda; (2) no licensed BDBV vaccine; (3) conflict-affected setting in Ituri limiting response access. The committee declared a PHEIC on 14 April 2026 — the eighth in WHO history — and issued temporary recommendations including enhanced border screening and accelerated vaccine access.

events.title: Active Response — 178 Cases, 52 Deaths as of May 2026
events.detail: As of 22 May 2026, the DRC-Uganda Bundibugyo ebolavirus outbreak has produced 178 confirmed and probable cases with 52 deaths (CFR 29%). The outbreak remains active across five health zones in Ituri Province (DRC) and two districts in Uganda. Contact tracing coverage stands at 83% of listed contacts. WHO has deployed 12 incident managers and three mobile laboratories. A second ring vaccination round is underway. Healthcare worker infections remain a concern, with 14 health workers among confirmed cases. DRC's M23-adjacent conflict zones in eastern Ituri continue to restrict response access to approximately 23% of the affected zone.

events.title: Outbreak Reaches Sixth Province as Africa CDC Warns of Record-Breaking Trajectory
events.detail: By 13 August 2026, the DRC-Uganda Bundibugyo outbreak had grown to 4,665 confirmed cases and 2,184 deaths (crude CFR ~46.8%), after a death in Buta, capital of the previously unaffected Bas-Uélé province, marked the outbreak's spread to a sixth DRC province. Deaths rose from 1,000 to 2,000 in under a month — the fastest fatal surge in Ebola's recorded history, versus over 12 months for the 2018–2020 Kivu outbreak and nearly 5 months for the 2014–2016 West Africa epidemic. Africa CDC Director-General Dr. Jean Kaseya warned the outbreak could become 'the largest in the world' if not stopped, while WHO said it was on track to surpass the 28,616-case West Africa epidemic as the deadliest on record. Confirmed cases sat just 35km from the South Sudan border along high-risk travel corridors. WHO and DRC were simultaneously advancing talks to launch a Phase 3 ring-vaccination trial of Ervebo (rVSV-ZEBOV) against Bundibugyo virus.

sources.name: European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC)

events.title: Outbreak Becomes Deadliest in DRC's History as UN Warns 'Ebola Is Winning'
events.detail: On 14 August 2026, UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher warned the DRC outbreak was killing one person every 30 minutes, declaring 'Ebola is winning in the Democratic Republic of the Congo,' and released an additional $30.5M from the UN Central Emergency Response Fund. Two days later, the DRC situation report published 16 August recorded 4,945 confirmed cases and 2,325 deaths, a toll that surpassed the 2,299 deaths of DRC's 2018-2020 Kivu outbreak — making this the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country's history and the second-largest ever recorded worldwide, behind only the 2014-16 West Africa epidemic (28,616 cases / 11,310 deaths). The case-fatality ratio climbed to roughly 47%, up from about 20% in early June, which CIDRAP and outside experts linked to strain on the response — late detection and community deaths — rather than a change in virus behavior. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the outbreak was 'moving faster than any previous Ebola outbreak' and on track to eclipse the West Africa epidemic. A second WHO IHR Emergency Committee meeting to review the outbreak's PHEIC status was scheduled for 18 August.

media.caption: The Bundibugyo virus outbreak has become the deadliest Ebola epidemic in DRC's history

events.title: Deaths Pass 2,500 as UN Warns Ebola Response Funding Will 'Run Out' Within Weeks
events.detail: UN Senior Ebola Coordinator Julien Harneis warned on 21 August 2026 that the DRC outbreak is spreading 'exponentially,' 'faster and wider' than previously observed, as the confirmed death toll passed 2,500 (5,290 cases, 2,516 deaths as of the 20 August situation report). Harneis said half of all deaths in the outbreak have occurred in just the last 20 days, and cautioned response funding is critically short: 'We're only covered for the next weeks, and very soon funding will run out.' A roughly 30% cut in humanitarian organizational capacity from recent aid reductions is compounding the strain, alongside more than 260 attacks on health workers recorded over six months (eight killed) and inadequate banking infrastructure to pay response staff in remote health zones. The US announced an additional $80 million to expand treatment-bed capacity and safe burial operations, bringing total US assistance above $592M. 160 healthcare workers have now been infected and 43 have died. The outbreak now spans six eastern DRC provinces, an area larger than France, with WHO modelling putting the probability of spillover into South Sudan at roughly 69-70%.

media.caption: Healthcare workers in protective equipment at an Ebola treatment centre in Bunia, eastern DRC

events.title: Outbreak Passes 100 Days as WHO Sitrep Puts Toll at 5,584 Cases, 2,680 Deaths; Africa CDC Warns True Burden Could Be 2-3x Higher
events.detail: Between 22 and 26 August 2026, the DRC outbreak passed the 100-day mark since its 15 May declaration. Africa CDC officials warned on 22 August that the official case count likely captures only 30-40% of true infections — meaning the real burden could be 10,000-15,000 cases — and that transmission may have begun as early as February 2026. WHO's Weekly Situation Report #15 (23 August) recorded 5,584 confirmed cases and 2,680 deaths across 57 health zones in six provinces, including two newly affected zones (Viadana, Bas-Uélé; Mutwanga, North Kivu). A joint WHO/UN 100-day assessment (24 August) documented major response scale-up — testing labs from 1 to 19, treatment beds from under 10 to over 1,300, contact tracing from 9% to 84% — even as roughly 60% of weekly deaths continued occurring outside treatment centers. The same day, WHO's second IHR Emergency Committee meeting voted to maintain PHEIC status and expanded 'high risk' guidance to nine bordering states including Burundi and the Central African Republic. The Washington Post reported 26 August that funding shortfalls and misinformation continue to hamper the response on the ground.

media.caption: 100 days into the DRC Ebola outbreak, response capacity has scaled sharply even as deaths continue to rise

events.title: UN Chief Warns of 'Virus of Indifference' as Toll Passes 5,700; WHO Confirms Uganda Outbreak Over
events.detail: Between 25 and 27 August 2026, two threads of the outbreak converged. WHO officially declared Uganda's linked 2026 Ebola outbreak over on 25 August, confirming completion of the mandatory 42-day monitoring period since the country's last patient was discharged 16 July — the outbreak totaled 20 confirmed cases (18 recoveries, 2 deaths). Meanwhile the DRC outbreak continued escalating: ECDC's tracker recorded 5,713 confirmed cases and 2,744 deaths as of 25 August (58 of 151 health zones across six provinces, CFR approaching 48%). On 27 August, UN Secretary-General António Guterres told the Security Council the world must overcome 'the virus of indifference,' warning the humanitarian response was only 48% funded and appealing for an additional $1.1 billion, with roughly 1 million people displaced in Ituri Province and more than 40 healthcare workers killed.

sources.name: European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control

media.caption: UN Secretary-General warns of 'the virus of indifference' as DRC's Ebola toll passes 5,700 and Uganda's linked outbreak is declared over
